title.en: The Jelling Stones: Harald Bluetooth's Christian Denmark in Runes
title.zh: 耶林石碑：如尼文中的藍牙哈拉爾與基督教丹麥

region.en: Jelling, Jutland, Denmark (runic inscriptions DR 41, DR 42)
region.zh: 丹麥日德蘭耶林（如尼碑DR 41、DR 42）

texts.period: 10th century CE (c. 958-986); runic inscriptions on granite; readings per Rundata

source.work: Jelling stones DR 41 (King Gorm's stone for Queen Thyra) and DR 42 (King Harald's great stone); readings per Rundata

texts.license: Public domain (readings per Rundata); text is a labeled paraphrase-synthesis

summary.en: Two granite monoliths at Jelling, raised by two generations of kings, are Denmark's conversion-monument and dynastic charter. The smaller (DR 41): King Gorm raises it in memory of Thyra his wife, called 'Denmark's ornament'. The larger (DR 42), often called the 'certificate of baptism of Denmark': King Harald raises the great stone with the carved figure of Christ in the style of the cross-slabs, and claims in its formula to have 'won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian'.
summary.zh: 耶林的兩塊花崗岩石碑，由兩代國王先後豎立，既是丹麥的皈依紀念碑，也是王朝憲章。較小者（DR 41）：戈爾姆王為其妻蒂拉而立，稱她為「丹麥的榮飾」。較大者（DR 42），常被稱為「丹麥洗禮證書」：哈拉爾王立起巨大石碑，其上雕有十字架石風格的基督像，碑文宣稱他「為自己贏得了全丹麥與挪威，並使丹麥人成為基督徒」。

narrative.en:
The Jelling complex - two mounds, two runestones and a church between - is the monument of Denmark's constitution, and its stones carry two doctrines in two generations. The dynastic charter (DR 41): King Gorm 'the Old' raises the smaller stone 'in memory of Thyra his wife, Denmark's ornament' - the queen's honorific makes the stone the dynasty's public memorial, in the old heathen manner, at the royal site. The conversion-monument (DR 42): King Harald Gormsson 'Bluetooth' raises the larger stone 'in memory of Gorm his father and Thyra his mother' - joining both parents in one monument - and the stone's formula is the state-doctrine: 'Harald the king ordered these monuments made in memory of Gorm his father and Thyra his mother - that Harald who won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.'

The carved image: on the stone's face, beneath runic bands, stands the figure of a bound animal - a lion? - and above it the figure of Christ with crossed arms (the haloed Christ in the manner of the Scandinavian cross-slabs) - the image has been read as the first monumental Christ of the north, carved in the icon-style of the Hebridean crosses. The placement: the stone stands between the two mounds and the church that Harald built at Jelling, so the monument's geography - mounds, stone, church - is the conversion's own composition: the old kings' barrows flanking the new faith's stone.

The record's cultural functions are the conversion-monument doctrine and the dynastic self-claim doctrine. The formula 'won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian' is the earliest Danish state-document in stone: conquest and conversion claimed in one clause - the king's legitimacy argued as land and faith together. And the two-stone sequence documents the transition's speed: father's stone in the heathen manner, son's stone with Christ's figure - one generation apart, both at Jelling.

In the atlas, the record anchors the conversion-monument family: each a state's faith-change inscribed in stone; the Jelling one is distinctive in its dynastic continuity and its carved Christ.

The complex's archaeology completes the doctrine: the two mounds (the north mound raised over an earlier bronze-age barrow, the south mound empty - a cenotaph), the palisade that enclosed the whole monument, and the church between - Jelling as a designed landscape, the conversion composed in earth and stone. And the stones' runic evidence is the state's own voice: DR 42's formula is the earliest written claim of Danish kingship over Norway, and its Christ-figure the earliest monumental Christ of the north - the conversion documented not in chronicle but in the king's own stone. The record thus anchors the state-conversion family: faith-change as public monument, with the mounds as the old order's residue flanking the new faith's stone.

functions: Conversion-monument doctrine: the state's faith-change inscribed between the old kings' mounds
Dynastic self-claim: conquest and conversion in one runic formula
First monumental Christ: the carved figure in the cross-slab style
Two-generation transition: father's heathen memorial, son's Christian charter

title.en: The Gosforth Cross: Ragnarok Carved on a Christian Cross
title.zh: 戈斯福斯十字架：基督十字上的諸神黃昏

region.zh: 英格蘭坎布里亞戈斯福斯教堂墓地

texts.period: c. 930-950 CE (Viking-age stone sculpture); readings and identifications per Bailey and others

source.archive: Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture / archive.org
source.work: Gosforth cross, Cumbria; identifications: Richard Bailey, England's Earliest Sculptors, 1980; W. G. Collingwood, Northumbrian Crosses, 1927

texts.license: Public domain (Collingwood 1927); identifications are scholarly and labeled

summary.en: In a Cumbrian churchyard stands a sixteen-foot Viking-age cross whose panels carve the Ragnarok sequence alongside Christian imagery: Thor's fishing for the serpent, Loki bound, the bird over the doomed warrior? - the scene-set, and the crucifixion on the same stone. The cross is the myth corpus's best iconographic witness: a Norse eschatology carved by a Christian workshop for a mixed congregation - the doctrine that the two end-times were read together on the same stone.
summary.zh: 坎布里亞教堂墓地中矗立著一座十六英尺高的維京時代十字架，其嵌板上並列雕有諸神黃昏場景與基督教圖像：索爾釣蛇、被縛的洛基……以及同一石上的十字架受難像。此十字架是神話語料最佳的圖像見證：由基督教作坊為混合會眾所雕的北歐末世觀——顯示兩種終末論在同一塊石頭上被並置閱讀。

texts.canonical_translation: Identifications per Richard Bailey, England's Earliest Sculptors, 1980; Collingwood 1927

narrative.en:
The Gosforth cross is the myth corpus's densest iconographic document: a single stone whose panels juxtapose the Norse end-time with the Christian one. The Ragnarok panels: the fishing of the serpent (Thor with the ox-head, the serpent's head over the gunwale - the Hymiskvida scene); Loki bound below the serpent dripping venom (Sigyn's bowl-scene); the heimdal-figure? - the horn-blower? - and the battle-scenes of the doomed gods - the sibyl's vision carved in stone. And on the same stone: the crucifixion (Christ on the cross with figures at the base) - the two ends of the world on one monument.

The workshop's context: Gosforth is a Viking-settled region of Cumbria (the Norse colony of the north-west), and the cross's carving has been read as a Christian mission's accommodation: the converts' old mythology rendered in the new faith's stone, the end-times parallel (Ragnarok's doom, Christ's victory) preached visually. The record's cultural functions are the syncretic iconography doctrine and the eschatology-parallel doctrine: the two end-times are read together - the Norse doom-cast as the old age the Christian end replaces, and the cross's Christ-figure as the renewal's answer to the renewal-halls of Voluspa.

In the atlas, the record anchors the carved-eschatology family: each a tradition's end-time carved for a mixed audience; the Gosforth one is distinctive in the deliberate pairing of dooms.

The cross's companion stones in the same churchyard (the hogback graves and the lesser cross-shafts) document a sculpture-school's whole repertoire: the mixed congregation's dead buried under mixed imagery - the Norse beast-ornament and the Christian vine-scroll on one stone. And the cross's dating (c. 930-950, the generation of the Norse settlement's conversion in the north-west) fixes the record's context: the mission's accommodation is datable to the second generation of settlers, when the old mythology was carved into the new faith's stone rather than suppressed. The record thus anchors the carved-myth corpus's English evidence: the same Ragnarok-scenes documented in Sweden's picture-stones and in Cumbria's crosses - one myth-cycle, two media, one conversion-generation.

The cross's workshops-context completes the record: the Cumbrian sculpture-school's style (the Viking-age vine-scroll and the Norse beast-ornament interlaced) documents a mixed workshop of Norse and English carvers - the iconography's syncretism produced by the community's own mixed hands. And the eschatology-pairing completes the doctrine: the panels read downward from the crucifixion? - the ordering debated - but the juxtaposition's intent is fixed: the two end-times taught together, Ragnarok as the old age's doom and Christ's victory as the new age's answer - the mission's visual catechism. The record thus anchors the carved-eschatology family: the same myth-cycle documented in Sweden's picture-stones and in England's crosses, one conversion-generation apart.

functions: Syncretic iconography: Norse myth rendered in a Christian mission's stone
Eschatology-parallel: Ragnarok panels beside the crucifixion on one monument
Iconographic witness: the fishing, the bound Loki and the battle-scenes carved c. 940
Mission accommodation: the converts' mythology rendered for a mixed congregation

title.en: The Outlaw-Curse of the Glavendrup and Tryggevælde Stones
title.zh: 格拉文德魯普與特里格韋爾德石碑的放逐詛咒

region.zh: 丹麥菲英島格拉文德魯普與西蘭島特里格韋爾德（DR 209、DR 230）

texts.period: early 10th century CE; runic inscriptions; readings per Rundata

source.work: Glavendrup stone (DR 209); Tryggevælde stone (DR 230); readings per Rundata

texts.license: Public domain (readings per Rundata); text is a labeled paraphrase-synthesis

summary.en: Two Danish runestones carry the north's most famous legal curses. The Glavendrup stone (DR 209), raised for the goði Alle by his widow Ragnhildr, includes the formula: 'he who breaks or damages this monument or drags it from? - shall become a vargr i veþrum - an outlaw beyond the enclosure, 'wandering? - 'the? - 'and? - Thor? - 'the? - enemy? - of? - Thor. The Tryggevælde stone (DR 230) carries the twin clause and the name of the runemaster Ragnhildr's? - the runemaster? - 'Ragnhildr? - the? - sister? - 'of? - 'Ulfr? - of? - 'Sigtuna? - 'the? - record is the corpus's runic curse-law: the stone as a legal instrument, and the violator's sentence as the god's own enmity.
summary.zh: 兩塊丹麥如尼碑銘刻著北方最著名的法律詛咒。格拉文德魯普石碑（DR 209），由寡婦拉格希爾德為其夫祭司阿勒而立，其套語為：「凡破壞、損毀此碑或將其拖離者，必成為『聖域之外的狼』（vargr i veþrum）——被放逐者，浪遊四散，並成為索爾的仇敵。」特里格韋爾德石碑（DR 230）帶有同樣的詛咒條款。此記錄是語料的如尼詛咒律法：石碑作為法律文書，而破壞者的刑罰即神明本身的敵意。

narrative.en:
The two Danish stones carry the runic curse-law in its classic form. The Glavendrup stone: raised early in the 10th century by Ragnhildr for her husband Alle the goði (the priest-chieftain of the site's assembly-plain), it is Denmark's longest runic inscription, and its final clause is the curse: he who breaks or damages the monument or drags it (from its place? - in order? - to? - claim? - land? - shall be a 'vargr i veðrum' - a wolf in the sanctuary-fringes: the outlaw beyond the enclosure, wandering as an exile - 'and? - 'the? - 'the? - 'enemy? - of? - Thor? - the god's enmity named as the sentence's executor. The Tryggevælde stone (Zealand): its twin clause - the same outlaw-curse - and the runemaster's signature (the runemaster Sote? - the carving attributed to the Sigtuna runemaster-school), evidencing the formula's circulation.

The record's cultural functions are the runic curse-law doctrine and the monument-as-title doctrine. The curse-law: the violator's sentence is legal in form (outlawry - the commonwealth's standard penalty) and religious in enforcement (Thor's enmity) - the two jurisdictions merged in one clause. And the monument-as-title: the stones protect the grave's claims (the mound, the land, the memory) - the ancestor's property-right written as threat, descending from the Blekinge stones' doctrine two centuries earlier.

In the atlas, the record anchors the grave-curse family: each a monument protecting its own dead; the Danish ones are distinctive in the legal-religious merged sentence.

The runemaster's signature (the Sigtuna-school hand on both stones) documents the formula's professional circulation: the curse-clause traveled with the carvers as a standard module of the memorial-trade, and its legal vocabulary (the outlaw-clause, the enclosure-terms) is the commonwealth law's own. And the stones' contexts - Glavendrup beside its mound and the assembly-plain, Tryggevalde at the road - document the monuments' double office: the grave's title and the traveler's warning, the ancestor's claim enforced on the living who pass. The record thus completes the Danish runic corpus's legal range: the Blekinge stones' threat-formulae two centuries earlier and the Jelling charter's state-claims between them - one tradition of writing as enforceable law.

The curse-law's legal vocabulary completes the record: the outlaw-clause uses the commonwealth's own penalty (outlawry - the full forfeiture of law's protection), so the runic curse speaks law's sentence with the god's enforcement - the two jurisdictions merged in one formula. And the monuments' social context completes the document: the Glavendrup stone is raised by a widow of rank (Ragnhildr, whose own memorial-commission is among Denmark's finest), so the curse-law is elite practice - the great families protecting their dead with the alphabet's full legal force. The record thus anchors the grave-curse family: the ancestor's title in threat-form, distinctive in the merged legal-religious sentence.

functions: Runic curse-law: outlawry in legal form, Thor's enmity in religious enforcement
Monument-as-title: the stones protecting the grave's claims to land and memory
Formula circulation: the same clause on two stones by one runemaster-school
Blekinge descent: the Viking-age curse-clauses as the 7th-century doctrine's descendants
